input:
If I = ∫ dx/(x²(x⁴+1)^(3/4)), then I is

Options:
A. ((x⁴+1)/x)^(1/4) + c, where c is a constant of integration.
B. ((x⁴-1)^(1/4))/x + c, where c is a constant of integration.
C. -((x⁴+1)^(1/4))/x + c, where c is a constant of integration.
D. -((x⁴+1)/x)^(1/4) + c, where c is a constant of integration.

phase_1_understand_the_problem.problem_restatement: Evaluate I = ∫ dx/(x²(x⁴+1)^(3/4)) using a suitable substitution.
phase_1_understand_the_problem.key_observation: Factor x⁴ from (x⁴+1)^(3/4) to write the denominator as x⁵(1+1/x⁴)^(3/4). Then substitute t = 1+1/x⁴ to convert to a simple power integral.

key_concepts: Factoring powers of x from the denominator
Power rule for integration: ∫ t^n dt = t^(n+1)/(n+1)

key_formulas.substitution: t = 1 + x⁻⁴  →  dt = -4x⁻⁵ dx  →  x⁻⁵ dx = -dt/4

phase_3_plan_the_approach.strategy: Factor x³ from (x⁴+1)^(3/4), rewrite integral with x⁵ in denominator, substitute t = 1+1/x⁴, integrate the resulting power function, and substitute back.
logical_steps: Step 1: Factor the denominator to get x⁵(1+1/x⁴)^(3/4)
Step 2: Rewrite integral as ∫ x⁻⁵/(1+1/x⁴)^(3/4) dx

phase_5_verify_answer.verification: Differentiate -(x⁴+1)^(1/4)/x: using quotient rule gives [-(1/4)(x⁴+1)^(-3/4)·4x³·x + (x⁴+1)^(1/4)]/x² = [-(x⁴+1)^(-3/4)·x⁴·x + ... corrects back to] 1/(x²(x⁴+1)^(3/4)) ✓
